Valtteri Bottas is decompressing from a disappointing DNF at Sunday’s Grand Prix in Malaysia by cycling some 350km to his next race.

It’s not the usual way Formula 1 drivers choose to recover from the mind-zapping fatigue and furnace-like conditions of a 300kph race in stormy Southeast Asia.

But it’s the way that F1’s elite gravel cycling convert has decided will work for him.

On Sunday night, Bottas completed “Leg 1” of a multi-day adventure ride toward this coming weekend’s Singapore Grand Prix.

The 37-year-old Cadillac driver had spun out on lap nine of a wet and wild race on the Sepang International Circuit on Sunday, which was being used as a substitute venue for the originally planned race in Bahrain.

Not long after stripping out of his overalls, Bottas clocked 56km in little more than two hours of night-time riding heading southeast toward Si Rusa.

The veteran car driver and Canyon bikes ambassador posted a video to Instagram showing him bumping his way across gravelly trails, followed by a #foodporn photo of a boutique dinner upon arrival in the popular tourist spot on the Malaysian coast.

With a base salary of around $5 million USD, Bottas hardly needs to “dirtbag” his journey, after all.

Bottas is famed for his off-the-racetrack exploits.

He’s been riding bikes for years and more recently integrated into the gravel racing scene through his partner, Tiffany Cromwell. He’s scored podium finishes at SBT Gravel and the Belgium Waffle Ride, and helped establish the FNLD GRVL event.

Bottas told his sponsors at Canyon earlier this year that he sees the bike as good for both his body and his mind.

“When I’m on my bike, I gain cardio, but I also use the bike almost like a stress release, you know? In a way, it’s a great way to clear my head if I have a bit of stress, and a chance to explore,” he said.

“It’s also a way for me to challenge myself when I’m not racing in my car. And when I miss racing, then I race on my bicycle.”

And while Bottas hasn’t spoken publicly about his trans-Grands Prix adventure this week, he must see it as a timely pressure release.

The long-time bike lover qualified for the UCI Gravel World Championships in Australia on October 11 after he finished fifth in his age group at the gravel world series event in Hlinsko, Czech Republic.

However, the champs had to go on ice for Bottas.

They clash directly with the approaching Singapore GP, where he and his Cadillac teammate Sergio Pérez will chase some much-needed points to claw their way out of the bottom of the F1 drivers’ championship.

Ezra Caudell, shown here this spring, has left a hospital after a month following his crash. (Photo: Gautier Demouveaux/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Ezra Caudell has left the hospital and is transferring into intensive rehabilitation some 31 days after his traumatic crash at the Philadelphia Cycling Classic .

The Modern Adventure Pro Cycling rider was discharged late last week and will continue his recovery at Magee Rehabilitation Hospital in Philadelphia, officials confirmed.

Caudell, 20, was already walking the hospital halls before his discharge , according to the recovery update shared by his family and team.

“Just as encouraging has been his neurologic recovery. Ezra continues to show significant improvement from the injury to his brain, with progress in his strength, cognition, communication, and independence each day,” an update read.

“His recovery will take time, but his progress over the past month has been remarkable, and to see him now walking, interacting with those around him, and moving on to rehabilitation represents an enormous milestone.”

Caudell crashed on August 30 while racing the Philadelphia Cycling Classic.

The move into rehabilitation marks a major step for Caudell, though the team update on Tuesday emphasized that a long recovery still lies ahead.

The medical team expects his lung contusions and his fractures to continue healing without the need for further intervention, officials said.

His family and Modern Adventure Pro Cycling thanked supporters for their continued support as the popular rider begins the next phase of recovery.

“Ezra’s family and the Modern Adventure Pro Cycling team have every confidence in him and remain deeply grateful for the continued support he has received,” a note read.

https://velo.outsideonline.com/news/lach.txt:
Morton during his 'Alt Tour' last summer. (Photo: James Startt/VeloNews)

Lachlan Morton , in his undying quest to check off an extraordinary ultra-cycling side quest every year, has announced his newest challenge.

Morton will set out to retrace the Pony Express, a foundational route of America’s westward expansion, on October 5.

The Pony Express was the historic route used to deliver mail from the eastern metropolises to the early settlements and cities on the western frontier. Like the horseback riders who relayed mail across the plains, mountains, and forests of the 1,966-mile trek from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California, Morton will travel light and fast.

Additionally, as those riders changed horses every 10 miles of riding, Morton will swap between his road, gravel, and mountain bike on a varied route that is built to resemble the historic route as closely as possible.

To raise the stakes, Morton will be racing the fastest recorded time set by mail carriers back when the Pony Express was in use in the mid 1800s.

“The way they could get mail across the country at that speed—before there was any railroad connecting it—was revolutionary,” Morton said in a press release. “The idea of people traversing such massive distances just captured my imagination, especially knowing a lot of that terrain.

“Think of these big open spaces—huge plains, mountain ranges—and you imagine a slow transition, but with the elevation and the vegetation it’s always evolving, and when you’re covering big distances you get a really diverse variety of riding. It’s a great canvas for adventure.

“It’s existed there for so long, and you feel like you’re participating in what the country is all about.”

The route will start in Missouri, take on the Great Plains of Kansas and Nebraska, before heading into the heart of the Rockies across Wyoming and Utah.

Perhaps the key of the journey, however, will be the long trek across Nevada—one of the most remote areas in the Lower 48—before Morton will finish through the Sierra Nevada, routes he knows well as he now lives in the foothills of California’s Gold Country.

While the route itself is not tied to any particular FKT or event, as his effort at the Tour Divide and Alt Tour were built from, his Pony Express effort will still have a time goal. Morton will be looking to beat the time set by the fastest Pony Express horseback relay.

In 1861, a team of riders and horses made the run from Missouri to California in just seven days and 17 hours to deliver Abraham Lincoln’s inaugural address to California to convince the state to remain a part of the Union as the Civil War loomed. That will be the mark Morton will hope to beat.

The Pony Express was replaced later in 1861 by the first national transcontinental telegraph line, but the mythos of the horseback mailmen lived on as iconography of the Old West. In his effort to take on the same route, Morton is hoping to understand more about what the true experience of the Old West was through the lens of his own riding.

“The appeal for me is the history of it,” he said. “It’s wild to get into that mindset—you’re a kid trying to make some money, and there’s this opportunity to ride a horse with a mochila full of mail through the night for 75 miles flat out, across remote, gnarly terrain that no one else has been crossing.

“It’s quite a courageous thing. It’s hard to imagine, and that’s why I want to go out there and try to get a better understanding of what that would have been like, and the difficulties they faced doing it over 150 years ago.”

Morton will be supported by his brother, filmmaker Gus Morton, who will be documenting the journey for a film and transporting the bikes that Lachlan won’t be riding over any given stretch.

Gus’ support will be limited, but with the remote nature of most of the course, when Lachlan swaps bikes, he will also restock supplies, just as the riders did on the old Pony Express a century and a half ago.

Taylor Phinney is heading back to track worlds (Photo: Tim Ireland/PA Images/ Getty Images)

Taylor Phinney , Kristen Faulkner , and Ashlin Barry headline Team USA’s selection for the track world championships in Shanghai this month.

The U.S. is sending a deep 17-rider roster to China as USA Cycling looks to build off of the back of unprecedented double-gold success at the recent road worlds in Montréal.

The 19-year-old Barry – who stampeded to solo victory at the U23 road race in Montréal last weekend – is joined by the 36-year-old Phinney in the seven-man endurance squad.

Faulkner leads the women’s team after she finished 21st in both the road race and TT in Montréal. The 33-year-old Olympic and PanAm track champion is joined by five more women on the U.S. endurance team.

USA Cycling is also sending four women to the sprint events after the team recorded a best-ever worlds finish last year in Santiago, Chile.

Phinney’s selection to the worlds team will stoke his dream of making a fairytale return to the Olympic Games.

The Coloradan came out of competitive retirement this spring with the sole mission of making it to L.A. 2028.

Phinney hasn’t raced track worlds since 2010, when he won the individual pursuit and hit the podium in the omnium. However, after winning gold in the U.S. national team pursuit this summer, it’s not out of the question that Phinney adds to a track worlds trophy collection that’s been gathering dust for 16 years.

The UCI track world championships run from October 14 through 18 in Shanghai, China.

Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

I recently saw a comment—I read all of them, by the way—asking why every cycling outlet posted about the latest Canyon Grail at the exact same time. It’s a common question, often followed by claims that we’re being paid. It brings up a fair point: why is there coordination when a new bike launches, and how does it work? There’s nothing nefarious, nobody is getting paid, and there’s a good reason for it. Let’s look at the Canyon Grail launch .

A month out, Canyon asked if I wanted to review the bike, providing only a launch date and time. I checked my schedule, decided the bike could be interesting, said yes, and sent over my size. Then things went quiet, and the bike didn’t arrive before the launch. It’s not entirely unusual for that to happen, but that’s why I didn’t have a launch-day review for you.

Instead, two days before the launch, I got a press release with specs and photos. That’s all I had, but it was well done with thorough information. I’ve also been doing this for a long time, and I bring plenty of banked up knowledge and experience. I read through the details, figured out how the bike fit into the broader market, and pulled out the nuances I suspected other outlets might miss but felt were important. I could have asked follow-up questions if needed, but the info I needed was there. I wrote the story and scheduled it for the embargo time.

You’ll notice everything revolves around that launch date and time. It’s called an embargo, and it’s the real answer to why everything looks so coordinated. An embargo simply means a media outlet agrees to hold its coverage until a specific time in exchange for receiving advanced information about a product. It might look a bit like a conspiracy, especially when every brand agrees to the same embargo, but it actually creates much better coverage for readers.

It allows bike brands to share information freely ahead of time so we get a chance to ask questions and genuinely understand a product. If I am able to get the bike ahead of launch, I get to ride it, take photos and video, and follow up on technical details. If there are no shipping or production hiccups, I have a fully tested, accurate review ready to go exactly when the embargo lifts.

Ultimately, embargoes prevent a race to the bottom. If they didn’t exist, the second I heard about a new product, I’d have to slam something onto the internet as fast as possible just to get people’s attention first. I wouldn’t have time to test anything or ask a single question. With an embargo in place, I can focus on the bike and make sure the story or review is actually worth your time.

Does knowing how this works behind the scenes change how you view launch day coverage? Hit reply and let me know if the coordination ever felt like a conspiracy to you.

All things being equal, the Canyon launch went pretty well. It wasn’t perfect, since I didn’t have the bike in time to publish a review for the launch, but I had the information I needed ahead of launch time. I’ll call that the middle ground.

A really great launch happens when there’s plenty of lead time. For the Pinarello X-Series launch earlier this year, I had exactly that. I traveled to Italy to see the headquarters and talk with Fausto Pinarello to get a sense of the company. I spent time riding the bike and had the people who designed it available for questions. If something didn’t make sense, the person who made the decision was right there with an answer.

Of course, I always have to remember that those people are inherently trying to sell a bike. They absolutely paint a rosy picture, and I have to lean on my knowledge to judge what reality is and what consumers will actually want to know. I always try to do this with an eye toward the ideal consumer: who does the company think this bike is for, and is it truly right for that person? When I’m at the headquarters with the designers, I have the resources to find that out and make that judgment.

When I left Italy, I had all the photo and video assets I needed, and was able to grab as much time as I needed with the bike. To me, that is the ideal scenario. Sometimes, I’ll get a bike sent to me and rely on video meetings with designers and lots of emails to understand it. That works too, and it can be nice not to travel.

On the other end of the spectrum, sometimes there is zero lead time. I haven’t heard from a brand, and I suddenly get an email exactly at the embargo time with a press release. I have to scramble to get an article up and hope the press release contains the details I need. Half the time it doesn’t and I find myself zooming in on website photos trying to spot things like a third bottle cage mount and waiting on the brand to answer questions. When that happens, the coverage is not as thorough.

I’ve already worked this into the article a bit so far, but what you have to understand is that everyone has the same information. What I try to do is look for the story inside of that information. Why does this matter to the reader?

I look for the unique selling proposition, then I tell that story. I typically like to share what the company storyline is—although not always unchallenged—and then react to that story. Sometimes I think a brand missed the best story of the product, sometimes I think the story makes sense and the people involved nailed it, and occasionally I think a product just does not work.…

Kenda has launched the Velora Endurance, a new set of endurance road tires that offer a premium feel with a range of puncture-resistant long-haul options.

The Velora brings durability and low rolling resistance to the table, with Kenda claiming major improvements in puncture protection and watts saved over its previous models. The model also comes in three sizes: 28, 32, and 35 mm.

With Kenda’s re-entry into the premium endurance tire market—in addition to other tires like the Silca Protocol RCR —the 32-40 mm range for all-road tires is quickly filling out. Not too long ago, that range of tires was a quirky grey area between road and gravel, but now it serves as another area of the industry where there are scores of good options.

Read on to see how the Kenda Velora Endurance fits into the mix. Hint: it’s one of the better options available.

While the Velora Endurance brings new options to the endurance/all-road tire market, Kenda is taking a fairly traditional approach overall with this model. It’s built, first and foremost, for durability.

That durability is derived primarily from the puncture-resistant base layer of the tire casing. Instead of loading puncture-resistance features into the entire tread, the base layer runs just along the center of the tread. This keeps the tire weight low and the tire relatively thin, despite the 35 percent improvement in the center tread’s ability to withstand debris and detritus.

While the Velora prioritizes the same puncture resistance as previous endurance tires, it is still a big evolution from the heavy, plodding endurance tires of years past. Kenda pairs the endurance-oriented puncture-resistant base layer with a premium rubber compound that is much more pitched towards speed.

To find this speed, the Velora uses the new K-Series rubber compound that has been slowly rolled out across several of Kenda’s recent new releases. That new rubber compound has been specifically formulated for performance on tarmac and yields a significant 12-watt reduction in rolling resistance compared to the previous Kenda endurance tire.

While Kenda also claims better rolling resistance compared to unnamed competitors, there is no third-party data yet for the tire’s overall rolling efficiency.

That being said, that compound is built to be both fast and durable. Kenda claims that the Velora Endurance is very wear-resistant, with a 27 percent reduction in tread degradation compared to the brand’s previous endurance tires. You could say the Velora is built for endurance in more ways than just long rides.

Lastly, while the tire is firmly a road tire, it does have prominent shoulder “siping” that runs in clusters along the tire. Those sipes, which are thin grooves cut into the shoulder of the tire, are specifically designed to help boost traction in wet environments. The grooves help funnel water away from the broad, slick center tread, which boosts traction especially on slick corners. The siping also helps add a bit of traction in dry conditions when riding on light, loose-over-hard conditions.

Over the last month, I have been able to put a few hundred miles on the 32 and 35mm versions of the Velora Endurance tires, and I have been very pleased with how the tires feel and perform in the right circumstances.

Personally, I felt more of a draw to the 35mm option as there are just fewer great options at that width. Additionally, as tires have gotten bigger, 30-32 mm is the range of width I use for race tires, so testing the 32mm—let alone the 28mm—just didn’t feel like it made much sense. Instead, having a nice 35mm endurance tire was the perfect pair for some adventures on the new Trek Domane, a modern endurance bike with clearance up to 40mm.

Would I have loved to try the Velora in 38-40 mm? Absolutely, but unfortunately, Kenda cut things off at 35mm. Nevertheless, I found the 35s had a great balance of versatility, reliability, and speed that really surprised me.

Out of the box, the Velora Endurance tires do look and feel like endurance tires. They have more structure, they feel on the heavier side, and the center tread is notably a bit thicker and more rigid than a pure road racing tire. But even with those attributes, the sidewalls felt fairly flexible. When I was mounting it onto the rim, the tire also felt more similar to a good racing tire than a rigid, heavier endurance tire.

Speaking of weight, the Velora is certainly no featherweight, but it holds its own. At 370g for the 35mm, the tire is about middle of the pack—similar to the Specialized Mondo, lighter than the Pirelli P-Zero, and heavier than the Silca RCR.

After the installation, I found that the tire felt alive straight away. There wasn’t any of the stiffness you might get from a tire with thick, new rubber. Instead, it rolled pretty fast and handled well, with the tire holding its structure even at a relatively low 50 PSI of pressure. One of my nitpicks with mid-width slicks is how inconsistent they can feel. The heavier, thicker tires can be too rigid and can be harsh and bouncy, neither of which inspires much confidence during cornering or at speed. Others are too light, and those can feel muddled and squishy at “all-road” pressure—even worse for confidence.

The Velora Endurance has a good balance between rigidity and suppleness. My guess is that comes from the tire’s split personality, with a fast rubber compound and strong-but-narrow puncture protection creating an effective pairing for that balanced handling.

The out-and-out speed of the tire is where things are less clear. The big test for the tire’s speed was a long Saturday group ride that functions a bit like a segmented race. The first two efforts are both uphill drags, a perfect scenario to feel a tire’s overall speed, before I would set off on my own up a gravel road and a long, steep gravel climb to test the all-road chops of the tire.…

It’s been just under a week since the 2026 UCI Road World Championships, and the paint shops at Colnago and Specialized have been hard at work.

To celebrate the two new elite world champions, Brandon McNulty and Demi Vollering, the champions’ bike sponsors have been hard at work to deliver them two unique liveries for the next year of racing. Interestingly, despite the two design teams working from the classic black, white, and rainbow color scheme, the two iconic brands have created dramatically different designs.

For McNulty, many fans will be excited to see that Colnago has gone beyond simply running it back with Tadej Pogačar’s design. McNulty’s Y1Rs has big, bold stripes on the front and rear of the bike, with a glossy black base. There are some other flourishes, but the oversized stripes steal the show.

Vollering, on the other hand, has gone much more minimalist. Her Specialized Tarmac SL9 is mostly white with clean accenting stripes of rainbows spread around the bike. Yet, the bike resembles Vollering herself, as it focuses on intentionality, and its flair is reserved for the fringes of the bike. Compared to McNulty’s Y1RS, Vollering’s Tarmac SL9 has a white base, with grey connective tissue.

We assembled the details of both of the bikes below, as well as a collection of some of our favorite rainbow bike liveries from the past few seasons.

To celebrate McNulty’s surprising Worlds win, Colnago has rewarded the American with a striking, bold rainbow design. The obvious showstopper is the amount of color on the frame. The design is anchored with a set of broad, clean rainbow stripes that cut horizontally across the bottom half of the bike. Like Pogačar’s Y1Rs, McNulty’s design has a black base rather than a white frame.

Beyond the bands, the black base itself has a few flourishes. Colnago coated the black base with a subtle glitter finish. That glitter doubles down on the glossiness of the look, while the brand says the effect is also a nod to the stars in the American flag as they glint in the sunshine. That kind of subtle extra detailing is also found in some of the other decals. The Colnago logo on the down tube, for instance, has an iridescent, holographic finish, adding to the shiny look of the frame.

Of course, Colnago is no stranger to outfitting a bike for the rainbow jersey. Pogačar, the winner in 2024 and 2025, had both a custom V5Rs and a Y1Rs. Nevertheless, in both cases it was a bit of a “less is more” approach, especially on his stripped-down lightweight Y1Rs we profiled at the Tour de France last year.

With McNulty, there wasn’t any subtlety—and why should there be!? If you look at the collection of custom bikes Colnago has made for Pogčar, they could fill several bike racks. For McNulty, this was the first. Boldness is imperative.

Compared to McNulty, Vollering has been striving for the rainbow bands for years. Her win was no surprise; it was the culmination of meticulous planning and tenacious riding that Vollering has leaned on for her career of success. Dutifully, Specialized has delivered a custom-painted Tarmac SL9 that fits that ethos.

“Winning world championships doesn’t just happen in one big moment; it’s thousands of small decisions leading up to it,” Emily Halwell, Concept Graphic Designer at Specialized, said. “This design celebrates that process. Riders spend years training, testing, and refining tiny gains, and the bike graphics reflect that. It’s a visualization of all those micro decisions building upon one another, ultimately leading to one goal: earning the rainbow stripes.”

Vollering’s design is mostly white with black Specialized details. The rainbow color was reserved for key areas of the frame, including the aptly named “win fin” on the back of the seat tube, the inside of the fork blades, and the top tube. Those rainbow colors on the frame, seat post, and fork are arranged in geometric patterns and lines that create an intricate design that can only be seen up close.

Throughout the frame, the design has a series of arrows, mathematical notation, and other notes that tie back to the Fastest to the Finish moniker, Specialized’s new central concept guiding its racing programs. The bike, in its small details, color flourishes, and design itself, is all about what the brand calls “the Equation of Speed.”

Even though the rainbow jersey was introduced in the 1920s, the rainbow bike is very much a 21st-century phenomenon. And, like so many of the fashion-adjacent cycling advances of the early 2000s, Mario Cipollini is at the center of it.

Cipollini only won Worlds once, but that was enough for him to change what it meant to wear the rainbow jerseys. The flamboyant Italian wore white shorts, rainbow bands everywhere, and had multiple Specialized bikes with big, bold rainbow decals. Love it or hate it, what is undeniable is how that look launched a new frontier for the rainbow jersey and everything that came with it.

Fast forward a decade, and cycling’s next master of panache, Peter Sagan, got three tries at the rainbow jersey and bike. Significantly, Sagan was a proponent of the bolder, black-based world championship bikes throughout his tenure in the rainbow jersey.

For many, the 2016 vintage of his rainbow Specialized Venge will bring back intense memories of envy. That bike can still be found in the annals of Facebook Marketplace, as the rainbow-bands-turned-camo will also loom large for a certain type of cycling fan.

One of the more underrated rainbow bike designs, and perhaps the one that is closest to McNulty’s design, is Mads Pedersen’s Trek Madone that followed his 2019 Worlds win. The bike was white, but was dominated by a broad, bold block of rainbow bands that cut diagonally along the front of the bike.

Perhaps it isn’t a coincidence that Pedersen’s unexpected 2019 victory is also the most recent example of a truly surprising result in the men’s world title.…

You requested road bike content, so this week you’ve got it. Last weekend was Worlds and the race for the rainbow stripes. Logan Jones-Wilkins was in attendance, and Mike Levy, Lisa Charlebois, and I handed him the mic for a breakdown of what he saw. We talk about Brandon McNulty and whether his World Championship win was out of left field or expected. We also discuss Kate Courtney and a ridiculous positional rule that could have completely upended the women’s race.

Before that, we start with some listener questions. We received lots of corrections on the Canyon mounting system, but I argue that the technicalities are irrelevant to the greater point. The Q&A gives me a chance to put on my family-man hat and share advice for riders trying to balance their mileage with time for their kids, while Logan answers for his Haro bike.

Later in the episode, we dive into a couple of topics close to my heart. We start by discussing why the Rapha financial meltdown is a textbook example of a marketing fail, while Logan presents a strong argument for why the recent CEO departure might have actually been a voluntary exit after all. From there, we pivot to high-dollar bling. The new titanium Firefly rim brake bike makes no logical sense in 2026 but still commands attention, while the $5,500 Partington wheels serve as a positive case study on how Western brands can maintain appeal against cheaper Eastern competition.
